subject: Accounting
title: Executive Compensation Ethics
description: A micro-lesson that makes Executive Compensation Ethics usable.

hook.text: A CEO earns $20 million. Workers earn $40,000. The ratio is 500:1. Is that ethical?

buildup.text: Executive pay includes salary, bonuses, stock options, and perks—often tied to financial targets.

discovery.text: When pay is tied to stock price, executives have incentive to inflate short-term results.

twist.text: Clawback provisions now let companies recover bonuses earned through restated financial results.

climax.text: Aligning pay with long-term value—not short-term metrics—reduces the temptation to cheat.

punchline.text: Pay for long-term value, not short-term tricks.

quiz.question: Why can stock-based executive pay create ethical problems?

details.summary: Executive compensation ethics examines whether pay packages for top leaders are fair, transparent, and aligned with long-term company performance. This topic covers stock options, golden parachutes, and the moral questions they raise.
details.whyItMatters: Poorly designed compensation creates incentives for executives to manipulate earnings or take excessive risks. The pay gap between executives and workers is also a growing social concern.
takeaways: Stock options can incentivize short-term stock price manipulation over long-term value
Say-on-pay votes give shareholders a voice in executive compensation decisions
Clawback provisions can recover bonuses paid based on later-restated financial results

faq.question: Why is executive compensation an ethics issue in accounting?
faq.answer: Executive compensation creates incentive structures that can motivate ethical or unethical behavior. When pay is tied to short-term metrics like stock price or quarterly earnings, executives may be tempted to manipulate financial results.

faq.question: What are clawback provisions in executive pay?
faq.answer: Clawback provisions allow companies to recover bonuses or incentive compensation that was paid based on financial results that are later restated due to errors or fraud, holding executives financially accountable for accurate reporting.
